name: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 1 (HNF4A-MODY)

clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNF4A, a transcription factor upstream of HNF1A that regulates beta-cell gene expression; inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance.
Clinically resembles HNF1A-MODY with progressive insulin secretory failure and marked sensitivity to low-dose sulfonylureas, which are first-line therapy in preference to insulin.

A distinctive feature is fetal and neonatal macrosomia with transient diabetic-range neonatal hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia in a subset of carriers, reflecting a biphasic effect of HNF4A on beta-cell function.
Unlike HNF1A-MODY, the renal threshold for glucose is normal, so glycosuria disproportionate to blood glucose is absent.
HNF4A carriers tend to have a lower serum HDL cholesterol and altered apolipoprotein profile compared with HNF1A-MODY, which can offer a discriminating clue.
Diagnosis should be considered in young non-obese patients with autoantibody-negative, C-peptide-positive diabetes and a strong multigenerational family history.
A macrosomic neonate with transient hyperinsulinism born to a parent with young-onset diabetes should prompt HNF4A testing of the family.
Genetic confirmation allows rational transfer from insulin to sulfonylurea in many patients and informs cascade testing of relatives.
reference.pathophysiology: MODY1 arises from heterozygous inactivating mutations in HNF4A, which encodes hepatocyte nuclear factor 4-alpha, a nuclear receptor transcription factor expressed in pancreatic islets, liver, kidney and gut. Within the beta cell, HNF4A sits within a transcriptional network that includes HNF1A and regulates genes governing glucose metabolism, mitochondrial function and insulin secretion; haploinsufficiency progressively impairs glucose-stimulated insulin release. The phenotype is characteristically biphasic: in fetal and neonatal life, altered regulation of the KATP-channel pathway can produce hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia and consequent macrosomia, whereas from adolescence or early adulthood beta-cell function declines and diabetes emerges and worsens over time. Because HNF4A also drives hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, carriers display characteristic reductions in HDL and apolipoprotein levels. Unlike HNF1A-MODY, tubular glucose handling is preserved, so the low renal threshold seen in MODY3 does not occur. Retained sensitivity of residual beta cells to sulfonylurea-mediated closure of the KATP channel underlies the strong therapeutic response to these agents.
additionalDifferentials: HNF1A-MODY (MODY3), the closest phenotypic mimic distinguished by low renal glucose threshold and normal birthweight
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (autoantibody positive, C-peptide low or undetectable)
Young-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus with obesity and insulin resistance
Glucokinase-MODY (MODY2) with mild stable non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia
Congenital hyperinsulinism from other causes in the neonate with hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of HNF4A (sequencing and dosage analysis), ideally within a MODY gene panel
Pancreatic islet autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) to exclude autoimmune diabetes
Fasting and stimulated C-peptide to demonstrate preserved endogenous insulin secretion
Fasting lipid profile looking for reduced HDL cholesterol
Documentation of birthweight and any neonatal hypoglycaemia in the proband and relatives
Detailed three-generation family pedigree for diabetes
HbA1c and self-monitored glucose to assess progression and treatment response
redFlags: Severe or recurrent neonatal hypoglycaemia in a macrosomic infant requiring urgent glucose support
Development of chronic microvascular complications, as the diabetes is progressive and confers standard complication risk
Abrupt loss of glycaemic control suggesting exhaustion of sulfonylurea responsiveness and need for insulin
Diabetic ketoacidosis, which should prompt reconsideration of type 1 diabetes
Pregnancy in an affected woman, requiring specialist planning for maternal glycaemia and fetal macrosomia
reference.prognosis: With genetic diagnosis and appropriate low-dose sulfonylurea therapy many patients achieve durable glycaemic control for years, though beta-cell function declines progressively and some eventually require insulin. Microvascular complication risk mirrors that of other forms of diabetes and depends on long-term glycaemic control.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the patient as type 1 diabetes and committing them to lifelong insulin when a sulfonylurea would suffice
Overlooking the diagnosis because glycosuria out of proportion to glycaemia (a MODY3 clue) is absent
Failing to recognise transient neonatal hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia as an early manifestation in mutation carriers
Attributing macrosomia solely to maternal gestational diabetes and missing the underlying monogenic cause
Not offering cascade genetic testing and counselling to at-risk relatives after a diagnosis is confirmed
management: Use low-dose sulfonylureas as first-line therapy in preference to insulin, exploiting the marked sensitivity of HNF4A-MODY
Transition many insulin-treated patients to sulfonylureas after genetic confirmation
Add or switch to insulin as beta-cell secretory function declines over time
Anticipate and manage neonatal hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia in carriers (for example with diazoxide) and associated macrosomia, monitoring at-risk newborns
Manage affected pregnancies jointly with specialists, with maternal glucose and foetal growth surveillance
Screen for diabetic microvascular and macrovascular complications with ongoing glycaemic monitoring
Provide genetic counselling and cascade testing of relatives for autosomal dominant inheritance
